summary: COSE defines signed and encrypted messages encoded in CBOR. This document adds the algorithm identifiers and key representations needed to use RSA with COSE, including RSA-PSS signatures and RSAES-OAEP encryption.

eli5.summary: COSE is a way to seal small digital messages. This adds one more kind of lock and key, called RSA, that people can choose to use.

questions: how to use rsa with cose
what are the cose rsa key parameters
what rsa key size does cose require
subtitle: The identifiers and key formats that let COSE messages use RSA signatures and RSA key encryption.

tldr.problem: COSE defines signed and encrypted messages encoded in CBOR, but it has no identifiers or key format for RSA algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers three RSASSA-PSS signature algorithms and three RSAES-OAEP key encryption algorithms, a new RSA key type, and the CBOR labels for every RSA key field, including multi-prime keys.
tldr.outcome: COSE messages can be signed and encrypted with RSA. Keys must be at least 2048 bits.

today: RFC 8230 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: What This Document Adds to COSE
sections.content:
CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE, RFC 8152) defines cryptographic message encodings that use Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR, RFC 7049). This document specifies algorithm encodings and representations so that RSA algorithms can be used in COSE messages.

It covers three things: RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) signatures, RSA Encryption Scheme with Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (RSAES-OAEP) encryption, and RSA keys. The RSA algorithms themselves are defined in RFC 8017.
sections.eli5: COSE already has a box for locked messages. This document adds the labels needed to use one more kind of lock, called RSA.

sections.title: RSASSA-PSS Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
RSASSA-PSS takes a hash function, a mask generation function and a salt length. Here the mask generation function is always MGF1, the same hash function is used for hashing the data and inside MGF1, and the salt length equals the hash output length.

Three algorithms are defined: PS256 (value -37, SHA-256, salt 32), PS384 (value -38, SHA-384, salt 48) and PS512 (value -39, SHA-512, salt 64). Implementations need to check that the key type is RSA when creating or verifying a signature.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a wax seal that only you can make. There are three sizes of seal, and each has its own number so everyone knows which one you used.

sections.title: RSAES-OAEP Key Encryption
sections.content:
RSAES-OAEP is an asymmetric key encryption algorithm, defined in Section 7.1 of RFC 8017. For the identifiers in this document, the mask generation function is always MGF1 with the same hash function, and the encoding parameters P are always the empty octet string. The key type MUST be RSA.

Three identifiers are registered: value -40 is RSAES-OAEP with the RFC 8017 default parameters (SHA-1), value -41 uses SHA-256 and value -42 uses SHA-512.
sections.eli5: This is a way to lock a small secret, such as another key, so only the owner of the matching private key can open it.

sections.title: RSA Keys in COSE
sections.content:
Key types are identified by the kty member of the COSE_Key object. This document defines RSA with value 3, and a structure for both public and private parts of an RSA key. Field names follow RFC 8017.

  • All keys MUST have kty equal to 3.
  • Public keys MUST have n and e, and every other field MUST be absent.
  • Private keys with two primes MUST omit other, r_i, d_i and t_i; all other fields MUST be present.
  • Private keys with more than two primes MUST have all fields. The third to nth primes are maps holding r_i, d_i and t_i, and other is an array of those maps.

All numeric parameters are unsigned big-endian octet sequences, encoded as CBOR byte strings (major type 2), using the minimum number of octets. The document supports multi-prime RSA, where the modulus has more than two prime factors, which lowers the computational cost of decryption and signing.
sections.eli5: An RSA key is a set of big numbers. The document gives each number a numbered slot so everybody writes them down in the same way.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the six algorithm identifiers in the "COSE Algorithms" registry, each marked Recommended: Yes. It registered key type RSA (value 3) in "COSE Key Types", and the RSA key parameters (labels -1 to -12) in "COSE Key Type Parameters".

The parameter labels are: n -1, e -2, d -3, p -4, q -5, dP -6, dQ -7, qInv -8, other -9, r_i -10, d_i -11 and t_i -12. All are byte strings except other, which is an array.
sections.eli5: IANA is the keeper of the official list, so every number here was written into that list and cannot be given to something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A key size of 2048 bits or larger MUST be used. The RFC says this corresponds roughly to the strength of a 128-bit symmetric algorithm. Implementations SHOULD be able to handle moduli between 2048 and 16K bits. Keys that are too large or oddly sized have been used in denial-of-service attacks, so key length should be checked before any cryptographic operation. Two remedies are given: do not use a key until a trusted party is known to control it, or let applications impose maximum as well as minimum lengths.

For RSASSA-PSS, a theoretical hash substitution attack exists, but using the same hash function consistently is an effective mitigation, and hash outputs are not truncated. For RSAES-OAEP, the SHA-1 default-parameter version is included because it is the most widely implemented set of choices. Keys MUST follow the constraints in Section 7.1 of RFC 8017, and keys with a low private exponent MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: Small locks are easy to pick, so use a big one. Very odd keys can also be a trick to make a checker work too hard, so look at the key first.

items.desc: The CRT coefficient q^(-1) mod p (bstr).

items.desc: The CRT coefficient for the ith prime (bstr).
